analysis.one_liner: Lets affordable-housing tax credit investors claim a second round of credits on existing buildings.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The low-income housing tax credit helps pay for rent-restricted apartments. Investors get credits for about a decade, and buildings must stay affordable for a longer compliance period — after which owners can raise rents to market rate. This bill would let an investor elect to keep a building rent-restricted for another 30 or 50 years in exchange for a fresh round of tax credits on that same building. The bill was introduced in late June 2024, referred to the tax-writing committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and investors in existing low-income housing tax credit buildings gain the most: they could claim a second credit period on buildings they already own, without financing new construction. Tenants in buildings whose affordability commitments were about to expire would also benefit if owners took the election, because those units would stay rent-restricted longer.

how_it_helps.text: Lets a building owner elect to extend the affordability compliance period by 30 or 50 more years in exchange for a new 15-year credit period on the same building [S2].

For buildings subject to an extension election, the bill counts those projects in the state allocation criteria for credits and exempts refinancing bonds for them from the private activity bond volume cap, making the second round of credits easier to obtain [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the additional credits, and the pool of credits each state can award is limited, so credits spent re-rewarding existing buildings are credits not available for newly built affordable housing.

drawbacks.text: The tax credit each state can award is capped, so paying a second round of credits on buildings already built would compete with credits for new affordable construction, potentially shrinking the overall supply of new rent-restricted homes [S2].
The bill directs a fresh federal subsidy to investors for buildings that are already built and largely amortized, a second subsidy on the same asset rather than new housing production [S2].
It was introduced with zero cosponsors late in a Congress already wrapping up, with no hearing scheduled, giving it essentially no chance of becoming law [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is preservation: buildings whose 15-to-30-year affordability commitments are lapsing would stay affordable for decades more. But the mechanism is to pay investors a second time for buildings the public already subsidized, out of a capped credit pool that otherwise funds new construction. Whether renters come out ahead depends on whether preservation is worth the lost production, and the bill does nothing to address that trade-off directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2024 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Wiley Nickel introduced the bill on June 28, 2024 [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax credits [S4].
No further action was taken, and the bill attracted no cosponsors [S3][S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill ever leaving committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, taxpayers avoided paying a second round of credits on existing buildings and the capped credit pool stayed available for new affordable construction. The LIHTC investor industry did not get the extension election it would have gained.

for.name: Rep. Wiley Nickel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party [S3].

industries.industry: Low-income housing tax credit investors and syndicators
industries.note: They would claim a fresh 15-year round of credits on buildings they already own, largely amortized, rather than financing new construction. Their gain comes out of a capped credit pool that otherwise funds new rent-restricted homes.

industries.industry: Developers of newly built affordable housing
industries.note: Credits re-awarded to existing buildings would compete with credits for new construction under each state's cap, reducing the financing available for new affordable units.
